solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Obscenely rich, sets meals out occasionally for a feast

indicators.note: something done obscenely is done in a gross, disorderly way, so these letters come out disordered

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: only coming out now and then means only every other letter is let through

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A vulgarly wealthy family occasionally lays on lavish meals as a banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obscenely rich' reads as a description of the diners, but it is an anagram of RICH; the odd letters of 'sets meals' supply the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas is the great annual festival, traditionally marked with a big celebratory dinner, so it is a feast in the calendar sense.

clue.text: Behaviour of channel under study

indicators.note: in a down entry, one thing placed under another simply follows it in reading order

parts.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn
a duct is a channel or pipe

explanation.surface: Someone is studying how a waterway or TV channel behaves.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' puts the channel below the study word, so it comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: Conduct is the way a person acts or carries themselves, a straightforward synonym for behaviour.

clue.text: Difficulty as end of stone is chipped off

indicators.note: a piece that is chipped off is broken away, so the named letter is removed

parts.note: a ruby is a precious stone
the final letter, which is the one taken away

explanation.surface: A stonemason's problem: the end of a block has chipped off.
explanation.walkthrough: The stone is a gem rather than masonry; drop its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: As in Hamlet's 'there's the rub', the word means an obstacle or snag, an idiomatic synonym for a difficulty.

clue.text: Guarantee I curtsey clumsily

indicators.note: a clumsy movement is awkward and jumbled, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone promises they will bob awkwardly before royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guarantee' looks like a verb in the surface, but it is the noun sense that fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Security is something pledged as a guarantee, such as collateral offered against a loan being repaid.

clue.text: Child-devouring god not left to skulk around

indicators.note: 'not' says the following letter is absent, so it must be taken out

parts.note: Moloch is the Canaanite deity to whom children were said to be sacrificed
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A monstrous god who eats children is lurking about somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the L from the ancient god's name to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To mooch is to loiter or wander about aimlessly, which is close to lurking or skulking about.

clue.text: Thus bird got food on river, its flow never still

indicators.note: in a down entry, being on something means sitting above it, so it comes earlier

parts.note: so means thus
a daw is a jackdaw
consumed food
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A bird fed on a river whose current never stops moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never still' is a pun: a still drink has no bubbles, so a liquid that is never still is fizzy.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda water is carbonated, so when poured it is always sparkling, the opposite of a still drink.

clue.text: Limited by obligation to accept uniform

indicators.note: whatever accepts something takes it in, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a bond is a binding obligation
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is restricted by a duty to wear a set uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limited by' reads as one phrase; 'by' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bound is confined or restricted within limits, as in 'bound by the rules'.

clue.text: Clumsy person comes up nervous and uncooperative

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means being read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lob, or lubber, is an awkward, clumsy person
shy means timid or nervous

explanation.surface: An awkward person turns up anxious and unhelpful.
explanation.walkthrough: LOB is an old word for a lout; bolshy is British slang, from Bolshevik, for bloody-minded.
explanation.definitionFit: Bolshy describes someone deliberately awkward and rebellious, refusing to go along with what is asked.

clue.text: Railway not smooth enough?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: insufficiently milled or polished

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: split the word as UNDER-GROUND, like coffee or a lens not ground enough.
explanation.definitionFit: The London Underground is the city's metro railway; something under-ground has not been ground finely enough to be smooth.

clue.text: Resentment as first of nights in prison turns into day

indicators.note: to turn into something else is to be swapped for it, one letter replaced by another

parts.note: a dungeon is an underground prison cell

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the first letter of the word, which is swapped out
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A prisoner grows bitter as the first night in jail drags on into the next day.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the first N of the prison word for D; the second N stays.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudgeon means a feeling of offence or indignation, usually in the phrase 'in high dudgeon'.

clue.text: Opera company on cue almost veto returning

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it
something returning goes back the way it came, so it is read backwards
almost means not quite all of it, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then shortened
to veto is to ban
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: An opera company comes in on cue, having nearly vetoed its own return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opera company' wants to be one phrase, but the opera alone is the definition. Shortened cue and veto go backwards together, and the company follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabucco is Verdi's 1842 opera about Nebuchadnezzar, famous for the chorus of the Hebrew slaves.

clue.text: Under false impression, law lord pitched into act

indicators.note: to be pitched into something is to be thrown inside it

parts.note: a deed is an act
Lud is the lord addressed as 'm'lud' by barristers in court

explanation.surface: A senior judge, wrongly believing something, is thrust into a bill in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like a statute, fitting the law lord, but it just means a deed. 'M'lud' is how British barristers address a judge.
explanation.definitionFit: To be deluded is to hold a mistaken belief, that is to be labouring under a false impression.

clue.text: Superior course in sport backed

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
something backed is run backwards, so its letters are read in reverse

parts.note: RU is Rugby Union
PPE is Philosophy, Politics and Economics, a degree course at Oxford

explanation.surface: A top-class course of study in sport has been supported.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby abbreviation turns round and the Oxford degree course goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Upper means higher in rank or position, as in 'the upper classes', so it is a synonym for superior.

clue.text: In part of speech adjust place at foot of page

definitions.note: 'In' is an example of the part of speech

indicators.note: in a down entry, the foot is the bottom, so the preceding part comes after the other one

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for page
to reposition something is to adjust where it is placed

explanation.surface: An editor tweaks the position of a word at the foot of a page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is not a link word here: it is the example that makes the definition, since 'in' is itself one of these.
explanation.definitionFit: Words such as in, on and under are prepositions, one of the traditional grammatical categories of words.

clue.text: Novelist's old letter kept by husband with reverence

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for husband

indicators.note: something kept by another is held inside it

parts.note: awe is reverential wonder
thorn is the Old English letter for the th sound

explanation.surface: An author's antique letter is treasured by a husband who worships the writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The old letter goes inside the reverence word, with the husband's abbreviation in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathaniel Hawthorne was the American writer of The Scarlet Letter, fittingly for a clue about letters.

clue.text: Handling foul matter at hospital department

indicators.note: something foul is messed up and spoiled, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: Staff are dealing with some nasty substance in a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foul matter' reads as one filthy thing, but 'foul' only signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Treatment is the way something or someone is dealt with or managed, so it is a synonym for handling.

clue.text: Then not half poorly received by celebrity, quite informally

indicators.note: whatever is received by something is taken into it
not half means one half is thrown away, keeping the other

parts.note: taken as written, then halved
fame is celebrity
poorly means unwell

explanation.surface: Then, half ill, the star was received rather casually.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the front half of the first word; the illness word goes inside the celebrity word.
explanation.definitionFit: En famille is French for 'in the family', used in English of doing things casually at home, among one's own.

clue.text: Jenny has no check on sprain

indicators.note: having none of something means it is missing, so those letters come out
'on' says where the unwanted letters sit, attached at the end of the longer word

parts.note: a wrench is a sprain or twist
CH is the chess abbreviation for check

explanation.surface: A woman called Jenny has had nobody examine her twisted ankle.
explanation.walkthrough: Jenny is not a person here: 'jenny wren' is the traditional name for the small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Jenny wren is the folk name for the wren, and jenny also means a female of some animals and birds.

clue.text: What's thought unlucky if one pushes forward in ceremony held in the north

indicators.note: something held in another is inside it
a letter pushing forward moves ahead of others, rearranging the order

parts.note: a rite is a ceremony
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Pushing to the front at a northern ritual is considered bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is I: move it to the front of the ceremony word, then place that inside THE N.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirteen is the number traditionally regarded as unlucky, hence superstitions about Friday the thirteenth.

clue.text: Choke as last of mouthful breaks tooth

indicators.note: breaking something splits it open, so a piece lodges inside

parts.note: a cog is a tooth on a gear wheel

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: Someone gags when the end of a bite of food cracks a tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: The tooth is on a gearwheel, not in a mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: To choke a pipe or passage is to block or clog it up, as leaves choke a drain.

clue.text: In prison could, having cut sleeves off jacket

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a cage is a prison

indicators.note: the sleeves are at the edges, so cutting them off keeps only the middle

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A prisoner could manage by cutting the sleeves off a jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: The sleeves are the outer letters of 'could'; a cagoule is a light hooded waterproof jacket, a British word.
explanation.definitionFit: A cagoule is a lightweight hooded waterproof jacket, a kind of anorak.

clue.text: Much harder at first to stab rodent: its tail cut off here?

definitions.note: the rodent's tail, in the nursery rhyme

parts.note: far means much, as in far better

indicators.note: a blade that stabs goes into its victim, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: a mouse is a rodent

indicators.note: a word at first contributes only its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter

explanation.surface: A violent scene: someone stabs a rat hard and its tail is severed.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme Three Blind Mice, the farmer's wife cut off their tails with a carving knife, so this is where it happened.
explanation.definitionFit: The farmer's wife in the nursery rhyme would live and wield her carving knife in the farm's dwelling house.

clue.text: Peer over there, near the start

parts.note: an earl is a peer of the realm
yon is an old word for over there

explanation.surface: Someone is told to look over there, close to where things begin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a verb meaning look, but it is the noun for a nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Early on means at an early stage of something, which is close to its beginning.

clue.text: Masses of stone parted by large implement

indicators.note: something parted by another is split open with it in the gap

parts.note: piers are solid masonry supports
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Great blocks of rock are split apart by a big tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large implement' reads as one item, but 'large' supplies a letter and the tool alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliers are a gripping hand tool, a pincer-like implement used for holding and bending wire.

clue.text: Bird in moult, one leg scruffy

indicators.note: something scruffy is untidy and dishevelled, so the letters are in disarray

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird losing its feathers looks bedraggled, with one leg showing.
explanation.walkthrough: Every letter of the words after 'in', with one as I, gets rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The guillemot is a black-and-white seabird of the auk family that nests on cliff ledges.

clue.text: Drunk, so wished to sleep?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the way the bedtime saying tells you to sleep

explanation.walkthrough: The bedtime saying is 'Good night, sleep tight', so this is the manner in which one is wished to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight is informal for tipsy, and the goodnight rhyme wishes children to sleep tight, meaning soundly.

clue.text: Car thief has no joy as passenger

indicators.note: having none of something means it is missing, so those letters come out

parts.note: a joyrider steals a car for a thrill ride
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A car thief gets no pleasure from being stuck as a passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: The thief's name literally contains the word to be removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is anyone carried in a vehicle, such as a bus or train traveller, so a synonym for passenger.

clue.text: Not the best financial package for student?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: falling short of perfect
second meaning, split in two: a university arrangement or bargain

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the split reading: UNI, British for university, plus DEAL, a package.
explanation.definitionFit: Unideal means not ideal, less than perfect; read as UNI DEAL it is a student's arrangement for university funding.

clue.text: Deficient blood in pale old pope

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: grey means pale or wan

indicators.note: something deficient is lacking a part, so a letter is missing from the end

parts.note: gore is spilt blood

explanation.surface: An aged pontiff looks wan, anaemic from lack of blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deficient blood' reads as anaemia, but it means the blood word minus its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gregory is the name of several popes, notably Gregory the Great, who sent Augustine to convert England.

clue.text: Sash somewhat too big

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the following words is used

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone's waistband is a bit on the large side.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the gap between the two final words.
explanation.definitionFit: An obi is the broad sash tied around the waist over a Japanese kimono.

clue.text: Offender shortly back in Clare's place

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction
said shortly means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a sinner is one who offends

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer, briefly, is back at the home of someone called Clare.
explanation.walkthrough: Clare is not a person but County Clare in the west of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennis is the county town of County Clare in Ireland, so it is a place belonging to Clare.

clue.text: House improvement free of strain?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an added room or wing
second meaning, split in two: no longer under stress

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the split reading: EX, meaning former or no longer, plus TENSION, strain.
explanation.definitionFit: A house extension adds space to a home; someone who is ex-tension has left their stress behind.
